existing_tips: 'Biergarten' is a uniquely Bavarian tradition of outdoor dining under chestnut trees.
'Dass' (that) introduces a noun clause – verb goes to the end. Often replaceable by dropping 'dass'
Separable: 'zuhören' – 'hör...zu'.
'gegen' (against) always takes accusative – no exceptions.
'Ostsee' means 'Baltic Sea' – literally 'East Sea'.
Without article: 'Heißer' takes strong nom. masc. ending '-er'.
No article (masc. acc): '-en' ending – adjective shows the case itself.
'Stolz auf' always takes accusative – 'proud of someone/something'.
V2 rule: the adverb 'Normalerweise' is element 1, verb 'frühstücke' is element 2.
'den' (acc. masc./dat. pl.) introduces a relative clause – its case depends on its role within that
Sentence adverbs like 'leider' (unfortunately) or 'natürlich' (of course) can start a sentence, trig
'Angst haben vor' uses 'haben' + dative – germans 'have fear' rather than 'being afraid'.
'Fix und fertig sein' – to be completely exhausted/done in.
V2 rule: 'Trotz des schlechten Wetters' is one element in position 1.
No article (neut. nom): '-es' ending – adjective must show gender/case.
'Die Brille' – feminine and always singular in German, unlike English 'glasses'.
'Überzeugt sein von' – 'to be convinced of' – always with dative.
'Der Lehrer' – masculine. '-er' ending for male professions.
'Neugierig auf' takes accusative – 'curious about something'.
'Die Katze' – feminine. Nouns ending in -e are often feminine.
'seiner Nachbarin' = dative fem.; 'helfen' takes dative object.
Accusative changes 'der' to 'den' and 'ein' to 'einen' (masc. only).
'Das Heft in der Hand haben' – to be in charge/in control.
'Zwei linke Hände haben' – to be clumsy with manual work.
'ein Brett vor dem Kopf haben' = to have a mental block.
